meta_description: Brain-computer interfaces explained in plain English — what they are, how an implant turns thought into a cursor, how they differ from a headset, and why the FDA just cleared the first pivotal trial.
og_description: A coin-sized implant turns thought into clicks — and this week the FDA cleared the first pivotal US trial.
og_title: Brain-Computer Interfaces, Explained — Daily Tech Briefing

paras: A brain-computer interface, or BCI, is a device that reads electrical activity from the brain and turns it into commands for a computer — so a person who cannot move their hands can still drive a cursor, type, or steer a robotic arm.

The idea is older than it looks. In 2002, a monkey controlled a cursor on a screen with a brain implant, and by 2012 researchers had a person with paralysis moving a robotic arm by thought. What changed is the hardware: the implants got smaller, wireless, and far more sensitive, and the software that decodes the signals got dramatically better.

Today's best-known example is Neuralink's N1. It is a coin-sized implant, about 23 millimeters across, that sits flush in the skull beneath the scalp. From its underside, 64 flexible threads — each thinner than a human hair — reach a few millimeters into the motor cortex, the strip of brain that plans movement. The 1,024 electrodes on those threads listen to the neurons there, and the implant sends what it hears wirelessly to an app that turns it into action. Its battery charges through the skin, and there are no wires coming out of the head.
sections.title: What it is

steps.d: Electrodes in the motor cortex record the electrical spikes of neurons as you try to move
The implant amplifies and digitizes the spikes, then sends them wirelessly to an app
A trained decoder maps the spike patterns to an intended movement or click
The cursor moves, a letter is typed, or a robotic arm reaches for the cup

paras: Every implanted BCI follows the same four steps:

1. Record — when a person with paralysis tries to move a hand, the neurons in the motor cortex still fire, even though the signal never reaches the muscles. The electrodes pick up those spikes. 2. Transmit — chips inside the implant amplify the signals, digitize them, and send them wirelessly to the app. 3. Decode — during calibration, the person imagines specific movements while the software learns which patterns mean left, right, or click. Once trained, a machine-learning model translates the patterns in real time. 4. Act — the decoded intent becomes a cursor movement, a typed word, or a robotic arm reaching for a cup.

The decoder is where most of the progress has come from. Neuralink's participants now reach a median of about 10 bits per second on its cursor test, with a record of 11.32 — roughly the speed of an able-bodied mouse user — and have typed at up to 40 words per minute. The company says it pretrained its 2026 decoders on more than 50,000 hours of participants' brain data.
sections.title: How it works: record, transmit, decode, act

paras: An implanted BCI puts electrodes inside or on the brain. It reads individual neurons, so the signal is sharp and the decoding can be fine-grained — enough for fast typing or speech. The price is brain surgery: Neuralink needs a small opening in the skull and a robot to place the threads, and the implant stays in the body for years.

A headset reads the brain from outside the skull, through the scalp. It needs no surgery, costs far less, and anyone can put it on — which is why consumer gadgets and research labs use it. But the skull smears the signal, so a headset can tell you roughly what a person is attending to, not which letter they want to type. For communication, the two are not in the same league.
sections.pull: A headset listens through the skull and hears a murmur. An implant listens inside and hears individual neurons — that is the whole trade.
sections.title: An implant vs a headset

vs.label: EEG headset
vs.text: No surgery, cheap, easy to wear. But the signal is blurred by the skull — good for attention and simple commands, not for typing.

vs.label: Implanted BCI
vs.text: Electrodes inside the brain read single neurons, so decoding is fast and precise. The price is neurosurgery and a device that lives in your head.

figure.alt: A person with a small implant on their head controlling a robotic arm that reaches for a cup on a table, glowing signals flowing from the implant to the arm
figure.caption: Thought to action: the implant reads the intent, the decoder translates it, and the arm does the reaching.

paras: The news peg is the trial. On November 25, Neuralink received FDA approval to launch the LINK Pivotal Study, the first pivotal trial in the United States for an implantable brain-computer interface. It will test whether people with severe paralysis from ALS can control digital devices by thought, with a focus on everyday independence. Enrollment is now open to adults in the US with ALS. The approval lets the trial proceed — it does not authorize Neuralink to sell the device — and the company is aiming for final FDA marketing authorization in 2029.

The field around Neuralink is moving just as fast. Synchron's Stentrode reaches the brain through a blood vessel in the neck, with no open brain surgery at all; its COMMAND trial showed patients texting and using iPads by thought, and it has connected its system to an Apple Vision Pro. Precision Neuroscience slides a thin film with 1,024 electrodes onto the brain's surface through a slit in the skull less than a millimeter wide. Paradromics' Connexus implant carries 421 electrodes and implanted its first long-term patient in June 2026. Blackrock Neurotech's Utah Array, the research workhorse since 2004, has supported decades of work on computer control and robotic arms.

The bet behind all of them is the same. Paralysis cuts the wires between the brain and the body, but the brain keeps sending the signals. A BCI is a detour around the break — and the first company to prove it safe and reliable in a pivotal trial gets to sell that detour as a medical device.
sections.title: Why everyone’s building one now

paras: Here is the catch. First, surgery is surgery. Neuralink's first patient, Noland Arbaugh, had some of the implant's threads pull out of the brain tissue in the weeks after his operation, cutting the signal; the company compensated in software, and its second patient had no thread retraction, according to Neuralink. Rigid arrays like the Utah Array can scar the tissue around them over years, which is one reason Neuralink chose flexible threads.

Second, a BCI reads one patch of brain, not a mind. Today's implants listen to the motor cortex, so they decode intended movement and attempted speech — not thoughts, memories, or feelings. Anyone promising a device that reads your mind is selling science fiction.

Third, the numbers are still small. Neuralink says more than 30 people have its implant, all in trials, and the device is investigational. The pivotal trial is the step that turns an experiment into evidence, and the evidence has to cover years of safety, not months. Cost and access are unanswered too: brain surgery, a robot, and years of follow-up will not be cheap, and who pays is a question for insurers and health systems, not just engineers.

And there is a question no trial can answer yet: who owns the data your brain produces. A BCI records the most personal signal there is. The companies say it stays with the patient, but the rules for neural data are still being written — the same week 42 state attorneys general fought to stop a bankrupt chatbot company from auctioning its users' private chats.

terms.def: Brain-Computer Interface: a device that reads electrical activity from the brain and turns it into commands for a computer.
The strip of brain that plans and sends movement commands to the muscles. Most implants listen here.
A tiny sensor that records the electrical spikes of nearby neurons. Neuralink's N1 has 1,024 of them.
Software, usually a machine-learning model, that maps patterns of neural activity to an intended action like moving a cursor.
Electrocorticography: recording brain activity from electrodes placed on the brain's surface, through the vessel wall or a thin film.
The late-stage clinical trial that proves a medical device is safe and effective enough for the FDA to authorize selling it.
